issues.legal_issue: A requisition order is not invalid merely because the public purpose for which the property is required is permanent in character.
material_facts: The property was requisitioned for a government undertaking's showroom, a public purpose of a permanent and perennial nature.
The challenge asserted that requisition was available only for a temporary purpose.
issues.conclusion: A requisition may be made for a permanent public purpose; the permanent character of the purpose does not by itself invalidate the order when made.
issues.legal_principle: Collector of Akola v. Ramachandra held that the power to requisition for a public purpose is not limited to temporary purposes. H.D. Vora v. State of Maharashtra concerned whether requisition could continue indefinitely, not whether an order was invalid from its inception because its purpose was permanent. Requisition and acquisition have different consequences: requisition transfers possession while title remains with the owner, whereas acquisition transfers title. This distinction is reflected in Entry 42 of List III of the Seventh Schedule and original Article 31(2) of the Constitution; Mangilal Karwa v. State of Madhya Pradesh and Chiranjit Lal Chowdhury v. Union of India were also referred to.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_requisition: A person challenges a government order taking possession of property by requisition.
predicates.public_purpose: The government requisitions the property to serve a public purpose.
predicates.permanent_purpose: The government requires the property for a purpose that is permanent in character.

issues.definition: When a requisition order is challenged, a public purpose that is permanent in character does not, by itself, make the order invalid.

issues.legal_issue: Continuing requisition may be a misuse of power where the government can acquire the same property, acquisition would serve the purpose with less inconvenience or damage to the citizen, and the government uses requisition without exploring acquisition despite having no insurmountable disability.
material_facts: The government had requisitioned the premises for a showroom and continued to use them for a permanent and perennial purpose.
The petitioner contended that the government could acquire the premises but had instead continued requisition to avoid acquisition compensation.
The Court stated that acquisition of part of a building was not absolutely barred under Section 49(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, subject to the applicable conditions and procedure.
The Court directed the government to take steps to acquire the premises if it wanted continued use, while allowing it to seek directions if insurmountable difficulties prevented acquisition.
issues.conclusion: Where both powers are available for the same property, using the more disadvantageous power without exploring the less damaging alternative may be a misuse of power in law; the government was directed to pursue acquisition if it wanted continued use, subject to the possibility of seeking directions if insurmountable difficulties arose.
issues.legal_principle: H.D. Vora v. State of Maharashtra establishes that requisition cannot be continued indefinitely and may cease to be valid after a reasonable period, depending on the circumstances. Read with Collector of Akola v. Ramachandra, the availability of both requisition and acquisition powers does not itself bar requisition. But where the purpose is permanent, acquisition is available, and acquisition can serve the purpose with less inconvenience or damage to the citizen, failure to explore acquisition without an insurmountable disability may constitute misuse of power. Section 49(1) of the Land Acquisition Act was relied on in directing steps toward acquisition, subject to its applicable conditions and procedure; the review order deleted references to the West Bengal Act 32 of 1955 as inapplicable to the case.

rule.if: challenge_to_continued_requisition and government_has_both_powers and permanent_need and acquisition_is_less_damaging and not insurmountable_disability and government_does_not_explore_acquisition

predicates.challenge_to_continued_requisition: A person challenges the government's continued possession of property under requisition.
predicates.government_has_both_powers: The government has power to requisition the property and power to acquire the same property.
predicates.permanent_need: The government requires the property for a purpose that is permanent in character.
predicates.acquisition_is_less_damaging: Acquisition can serve the government's purpose while causing less inconvenience or damage to the affected citizen than continued requisition.
predicates.insurmountable_disability: The government faces an insurmountable obstacle to acquiring the property.
predicates.government_does_not_explore_acquisition: The government continues requisition without exploring the available power to acquire the property.

issues.definition: When a continuing requisition is challenged, it is misuse of power if the government has both powers, has a permanent need, can achieve its purpose through the less damaging alternative, faces no insurmountable obstacle, and does not explore acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: Long duration and a permanent purpose, without additional supporting material, do not alone establish that a requisition was initially invalid or that its continuation became mala fide or colourable.
material_facts: The premises had remained under requisition for over 25 years for a showroom serving a permanent and perennial purpose.
The requisition served a public purpose.

The Court found that those circumstances, without further material, did not support an inference that the requisition was initially improper or that its continuation had become mala fide or colourable.
issues.conclusion: The requisition order was upheld and its continuation was permitted subject to directions to pursue acquisition if continued use was wanted; if insurmountable difficulties prevented acquisition, the government could seek appropriate directions.
issues.legal_principle: Under H.D. Vora v. State of Maharashtra, whether a requisition has continued beyond a reasonable period depends on the facts and circumstances. Collector of Akola v. Ramachandra establishes that a permanent purpose does not by itself invalidate requisition. The Court held that lapse of time and a permanent purpose alone do not establish bad faith or colourable exercise; further material is required. It upheld continuation subject to acquisition-related directions under Section 49(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, with the review order deleting references to the West Bengal Act 32 of 1955 as inapplicable.

rule.if: challenge_to_requisition and requisition_is_longstanding and permanent_purpose and public_purpose and no_additional_material_supports_bad_faith

predicates.challenge_to_requisition: A person challenges a government order requisitioning property or its continued operation.
predicates.requisition_is_longstanding: The government has kept the property under requisition for an extended period.
predicates.permanent_purpose: The government requires the property for a purpose that is permanent in character.
predicates.public_purpose: The requisition serves a public purpose.
predicates.no_additional_material_supports_bad_fait: No material beyond the requisition's duration and the permanent character of its purpose supports an inference of bad faith or colourable exercise.

issues.definition: When a public-purpose requisition has continued for an extended period for a permanent purpose, but no additional material supports bad faith, the requisition remains upheld subject to acquisition efforts.
